answer.label: Not the Bible — an English proverb
answer.authorDates: 1605–1682 · English physician & author — first known to print the phrase, and against it
answer.sourceLine: No verse of the King James Bible contains this sentence — a KJV keyword search for “charity begins” returns nothing, and the nearest text, 1 Timothy 5:8, says something different. Its earliest known printing in this exact wording is Sir Thomas Browne’s Religio Medici, Part the Second, Sect. 4 — printed without his consent in 1642, authorised in 1643 — where Browne quotes it as “the voice of the world” and then argues against it.

source.heading: The earliest known printing

docMeta.dd: Religio Medici, Part the Second, Sect. 4
Printed without the author’s consent in 1642; first authorised edition 1643. Text below from the 1682 edition, the last in his lifetime.
Quoted by Browne as “the voice of the world” — a proverb already in circulation, which he rejects.

source.excerpt: But how shall we expect charity towards others, when we are uncharitable to ourselves? “Charity begins at home,” is the voice of the world; yet is every man his greatest enemy, and as it were his own executioner.
trail: Before the modern wording. Phrase Finder traces the idea to John Wyclif’s Of Prelates (1382), “Charite schuld bigyne at hem-self,” and the first pairing of charity with home to John Marston’s play Histrio-Mastix, published 1610 (Phrase Finder ↗).

1642/1643 — into print. Browne’s Religio Medici carries the sentence in Part the Second, Sect. 4; the Project Gutenberg text, taken from the 1682 edition, notes that the first genuine edition appeared in 1643 after the book had been “surreptitiously printed” (full text ↗). Wikiquote’s sourced entry cites it to Religio Medici (1643), Part II, Section 4 (Wikiquote ↗).

The Bible check. No King James verse contains the phrase; the closest, 1 Timothy 5:8, reads “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1 Timothy 5, KJV ↗).

The Terence trail. The classical credit comes from a translator’s note, not from Terence: Henry T. Riley’s footnote to a line of the Andria calls it “Equivalent to our sayings, ‘Charity begins at home;’ ‘Take care of number one’” (Riley’s Terence ↗).

source.excerptNote: The proverb returns in the next section, where Browne writes that dying for a friend “seems strange to vulgar affections and such as confine themselves within that worldly principle, ‘Charity begins at home.’”

source.rightsNote: Religio Medici was printed in 1642 and issued in an authorised edition in 1643; the text quoted here is the 1682 edition, the last published in Browne’s lifetime. All are far earlier than 1931, and the work is in the public domain in the United States — the Project Gutenberg edition linked above is distributed on that basis. author.name: Sir Thomas Browne
author.heading: The doctor who quoted the proverb in order to disagree with it
author.bio: Sir Thomas Browne was an English polymath and author whose works range across science, medicine, religion and the esoteric. Religio Medici — “the religion of a physician” — was his first and most celebrated book: he never meant to publish it, an unauthorised printing appeared in 1642, and he issued an authorised edition in 1643. He is the first writer known to have put “Charity begins at home” into print, which is not the same as coining it: he quotes it as a saying everyone already used, and calls it, a page later, that worldly principle.

misattribution.heading: Where the credits go wrong
misattribution.intro: Two attributions dominate: Scripture, and the Roman playwright Terence. Neither survives contact with the texts.

items.why: A King James keyword search for “charity begins” returns no results. The passage usually meant is 1 Timothy 5:8 — “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” — a command about providing for dependants, not the proverb (1 Timothy 5, KJV ↗).

Quote sites credit Terence’s Andria. What Terence’s character actually says, in Henry T. Riley’s literal English version, is “Look you, I am the most concerned in my own interests” — and it is Riley’s own footnote, not Terence, that calls this “Equivalent to our sayings, ‘Charity begins at home;’ ‘Take care of number one’” (Riley’s Terence, footnote 75 ↗). Quote/Counterquote makes the same point about this footnote seeding the credit (Quote/Counterquote ↗).

Browne is the earliest writer known to print the modern wording, but he attributes it to everybody: it is “the voice of the world,” and in the next section “that worldly principle” — a view he sets himself against (Religio Medici, Part the Second ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous English proverb, already current when Sir Thomas Browne put it into print in Religio Medici to disagree with it — not Scripture, and not Terence (Wikiquote, sourced ↗).

context.heading: A proverb that says the opposite of what its most famous printing meant
lead: “Charity begins at home” is normally deployed to close a door: look after your own before you look after strangers. The sentence’s first known appearance in print does exactly the reverse. In Religio Medici, Browne sets it up as a saying he is about to knock down — “But how shall we expect charity towards others, when we are uncharitable to ourselves? ‘Charity begins at home,’ is the voice of the world” — and a section later he dismisses those “as confine themselves within that worldly principle” when weighing whether a man might lay down his life for a friend.

The Bible credit is a category error rather than a translation quirk. Scripture does contain a related instruction — 1 Timothy 5:8, in the King James wording, warns against the man who “provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house” — but that is a duty of provision, not the modern proverb, and no King James verse uses the phrase. The English saying seems to have grown up alongside the idea rather than out of any single verse.
context.detailsSummary: What Browne actually argues in the surrounding pages
detailsBody: Sect. 4 of Part the Second opens on self-love as the thing everyone condemns and everyone practises, and moves from there to the complaint “that charity grows cold.” The proverb arrives as evidence for the prosecution: the world says charity begins at home, “yet is every man his greatest enemy, and as it were his own executioner.”

In Sect. 5 the phrase returns explicitly as a limit on friendship: laying down one’s life for a friend, Browne writes, “seems strange to vulgar affections and such as confine themselves within that worldly principle, ‘Charity begins at home.’” Both passages are in the 1682 text, the last edition published in his lifetime.
context.pull: “Charity begins at home” is the voice of the world — Browne’s phrase for a view he did not share.

sourcesVerified.claim: Religio Medici, Part the Second, Sect. 4 contains: 'But how shall we expect charity towards others, when we are uncharitable to ourselves? "Charity begins at home," is the voice of the world; yet is every man his greatest enemy, and as it were his own executioner.' — and Sect. 5 repeats it as 'that worldly principle'.

The same Gutenberg edition's preface states the text is taken from the 1682 edition, the last in the author's lifetime, and that the first genuine edition appeared in 1643 after the book was surreptitiously printed.
The sentence 'Charity begins at home, is the voice of the World; yet is every man his greatest enemy, and, as it were, his own Executioner' appears in Browne's Religio Medici.
Wikiquote's sourced entry gives the quotation and cites it to Religio Medici (1643), Part II, Section 4.

Phrase Finder states the phrase is not biblical, that Wyclif expressed the idea in 1382 in Of Prelates ('Charite schuld bigyne at hem-self'), that Marston's Histrio-Mastix (published 1610) first connects charity and home, and that Browne was first to put the modern form into print.

1 Timothy 5:8 (KJV) reads 'But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel'; 5:4 reads 'let them learn first to shew piety at home'.
A King James Version keyword search for 'charity begins' returns no Bible verse results.

In Henry T. Riley's translation of Terence (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1896), Andria Act IV, Scene I renders the line 'Look you, I am the most concerned in my own interests', and Riley's footnote 75 to that line (Ver. 637) reads 'Equivalent to our sayings, "Charity begins at home;" "Take care of number one."'
Wiktionary defines the proverb and gives an illustrative quotation dated 1643 from Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici.
Thomas Browne's dates are 19 October 1605 – 19 October 1682; an unauthorised edition of Religio Medici appeared in 1642 and an authorised version in 1643.
Religio Medici was published in 1643 after an unauthorised version was distributed the previous year.
The saying is wrongly attributed to Terence; the actual Latin line is 'Proximus sum egomet mihi', and Riley's footnote equating it with 'Charity begins at home' is what created the attribution.
Wikiquote's Terence page gives 'Look you, I am the most concerned in my own interests' as Andria, Act IV, scene 1, line 12.
